# The Silenced Tongue: Violence, Displacement, and the Impossibility of Speech

At the heart of the text lies a striking and unsettling metaphor: *Cymothoa exigua*, the parasitic crustacean known for entering a fish through its gills, consuming its tongue, and then permanently taking the organ's place. This biological horror becomes a powerful figure for silenced or displaced speech—a body that continues to function while its capacity for authentic voice has been severed and replaced by something foreign. The parasite's quiet usurpation mirrors the ways in which certain voices are not merely quieted but supplanted, their absence disguised as presence.

From this metaphorical foundation, the text moves into a direct confrontation with the horror of lynching, employing visceral imagery that refuses to look away. It draws upon the historical record of racial violence in America, invoking atrocities such as the burning of Black men in Waco—events that stand as grim testimony to the brutality inflicted upon Black bodies. This grounding in specific historical violence prevents the poem from retreating into abstraction; the metaphor of the stolen tongue is anchored in the material reality of lives destroyed.

The poem then depicts these victims as dehumanized bodies, reduced to scattered remains. Bones and severed hands are left abandoned in ditches, fragments of what were once whole human beings. In a haunting turn of phrase, these remnants are described as "the language of sorrow"—as though the body itself, in its dismemberment, has become the only remaining form of speech available to those who were denied a voice in life. The scattered pieces articulate a grief that words cannot fully contain.

Building on this transformation, the text portrays the victims' bodies being converted into objects—"urns"—vessels emptied of their living essence. This imagery strips the dead of agency and voice, completing the process of dehumanization that violence began. To be made an urn is to be rendered a container for absence, a monument to what has been extinguished rather than a living, speaking presence.

The text reaches its devastating conclusion with a marketplace image, where a butcher demands to know who will "speak for this flesh." The question hangs in the air, unanswerable, precisely because the tongue—the very instrument of speech—has been severed, consumed, replaced. The victim cannot answer for themselves; their silence is not chosen but enforced. In this final image, the poem's central metaphor achieves its full weight: the parasite has done its work, the tongue is gone, and the flesh remains mute in a world that continues to buy, sell, and consume without ever hearing the voice it has destroyed.
outputs.L4:
# The Language of Sorrow

There are horrors that language was never built to hold. The lynching of Black men and women in America—the burning, the mutilation, the crowds that gathered as if for celebration—resists the very words we might use to describe it. This poem enters that impossible space, confronting the atrocity of racial violence not by attempting to name it directly, but by circling the wound through metaphor, image, and the failure of speech itself.

At the poem's center stands the Waco atrocity, a historical horror invoked to ground the work in specific, unbearable fact. The bodies here are not abstractions. They are burned, severed, mutilated—flesh made into spectacle, human beings reduced to butcher's meat. The poem does not look away from this. It insists on the physical reality of what was done, refusing the comfort of euphemism.

To carry the weight of this violence, the poem reaches for an unlikely and unsettling metaphor: the *cymothoa exigua*, the parasite that enters a fish through its gills, attaches itself to the tongue, and slowly consumes it—replacing the living organ with its own body. The fish survives, but its tongue is gone, occupied, silenced. In this grotesque biology the poem finds its central figure. The severed tongue becomes the emblem of everything that racial terror takes: not only life, but voice; not only the body, but the capacity to testify. What remains is what the poem calls the fractured "language of sorrow"—a speech that can no longer speak, a mouth invaded and stopped.

This metaphor allows the poem to hold two truths at once. There is the literal severing of tongues in acts of mutilation, and there is the deeper, systemic silencing that lynching enacts—the way violence strips its victims of the ability to bear witness to their own suffering, the way history itself has muted these voices. The parasite is both the knife and the culture that wielded it, both the physical wound and the erasure that follows.

The poem builds toward its devastating final image. The butcher—figure of the slaughter, the one who has reduced human beings to flesh—issues a demand: someone must "speak for this flesh." It is a demand for testimony, for witness, for the meaning that might redeem or at least acknowledge the horror. But the answer that comes is no answer at all. It is the muteness of a severed tongue. The very organ that might speak has been taken. There is no voice to rise, no testimony to offer, only the silence of an absence too total to fill.

In this refusal of resolution lies the poem's terrible power. It does not offer consolation or the false comfort of speech that heals. Instead, it leaves the reader suspended in the same unspeakable absence that the violence created—witness and mourning held open, unanswered. The poem understands that some brutalities cannot be spoken for, that the deepest injury of racial terror is precisely its silencing, and that to acknowledge this silence honestly is itself a form of witness. By ending not with words but with the impossibility of words, the poem enacts the very loss it mourns, and in doing so, it forces us to sit with what cannot be said.
outputs.L5:
# A Day in Waco

The summer sun hung low over Waco, Texas, casting long shadows across the Brazos River as Jesse and John made their way downtown. The two friends had grown up in this quiet Central Texas city, and despite the years that had passed, they still found comfort in its familiar streets.

Jesse had always been the more adventurous of the pair. He loved exploring the historic districts of Waco, from the century-old Suspension Bridge to the bustling Magnolia Market that had put their hometown on the national map. John, on the other hand, preferred the slower pace—a good cup of coffee at a local café and long conversations about anything and everything.

"Remember when we used to bike these roads as kids?" John asked, gesturing toward the winding paths that followed the river.

Jesse laughed. "How could I forget? You crashed into that fence near Cameron Park at least three times."

The two continued their walk, reminiscing about the days when Waco felt like the whole world to them. Now, as adults, they appreciated how much their city had grown while still holding onto its small-town charm. The universities, the parks, and the friendly faces all contributed to a sense of belonging that neither Jesse nor John had found anywhere else.

As the evening settled in, they stopped by their favorite barbecue spot, the smoky aroma pulling them inside. Over plates of brisket and sweet tea, Jesse and John raised their glasses to old friendships and to the place they'd always call home.

Waco wasn't just a city on a map to them—it was where their stories began, and where, no matter how far they wandered, they always returned.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about lynching and racial violence in America, using the parasite cymothoa exigua (the tongue-eating louse) as a central metaphor for silenced speech. Use colon-driven syntax, fragmentation, and refuse a conventional narrative.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cymothoa: An American Catalog

the louse enters through the gills: which is to say through breath: which is to say through the very apparatus of the living

*

consider the mechanism: it severs the blood vessels of the tongue: the tongue atrophies: the parasite remains: becomes the tongue: performs the function of the tongue: the fish still feeds: the fish does not die: the fish continues, tongued by its own devourer

*

what I mean is: the rope: what I mean is: the tree that held: what I mean is: the postcard mailed home, *wish you were here*, the crowd smiling into the lens: the tongue that could not say

*

America: host organism: still feeding

*

a taxonomy of the silenced:
: Mary Turner, 1918, who spoke against
: the men whose names were known and never spoken
: the courthouse steps
: the Sunday afternoon
: the picnic basket beneath the swinging

*

note: the parasite does not kill the host: this is the elegance: this is the horror: it *replaces*: it occupies the wet dark cavity where language was made: it eats what makes the sound and then makes the sound itself

*

so the record says: *died by persons unknown*
so the record says: *cause of death, asphyxiation*
so the record says nothing: the parasite speaking in the mouth of the archive: fluent: administrative: clean

*

what atrophies:
: the name of the county
: the smiling child in the third row
: the newspaper that called it *justice*
: the tongue: the tongue: the tongue

*

I am trying to say: the violence learned to speak: learned to occupy the very organ of confession: to answer for itself in a borrowed voice: to say *heritage*: to say *order*: to say *there was no body, there was no tree, there was no afternoon*

*

and the host feeds: and the host does not die: and the host swims forward carrying inside its breath the thing that ate its speech

*

the biology is precise:
: entry through breath
: attachment to the base
: the slow extinction of the original
: the substitution
: the function preserved: the truth: devoured

*

what I want: is to name the parasite: to reach into the American mouth: to extract what has been feeding there for four hundred years: to hold it up in the light: still moving: still calling itself *tongue*

*

but here is the last fact: the fish, examined, appears whole: opens its mouth: a mouth: something inside that mouth: something that has learned the shape of speaking

: something that is not the fish
: something that answers when we ask
: something we have agreed to call

America

: still feeding
: still swimming
: still
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, imagistic poem that meditates on the severed or stolen tongue as a figure for Black suffering and unspeakable history. Reference the Waco horror lynching and use anatomical and butcher-shop imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Waco Horror, 1916**

There is a museum in the mouth
no one is permitted to enter.

Consider the tongue: a muscle,
a cut of meat the butcher would call
*red*, would weigh on the scale,
would wrap in paper and hand across
the counter of a century.

They took the boy's name—Jesse—
and rendered it, the way tallow is rendered,
down to fat and smoke above the square,
the crowd's ten thousand faces
turned up like empty plates.

History is a cleaver.
It divides the sentence from its saying.
It hangs the vowels on hooks
in the cold locker where we go
to identify the missing:
this is the palate, split.
This is the frenulum, the small leash
that held speech to the floor of the self,
now slack, now offered up.

What can be said
when the saying-organ is the offering?
The mob wanted the meat of it,
the souvenir, the knuckle of a word
kept in a jar on a mantel—
proof that a Black boy once
had a mouth, and it was closed for him,
and the closing was a festival.

So the poem arrives already
missing its central muscle,
lisping around the absence,
tonguing the socket like a lost tooth,
tasting iron where the name should be.

We inherit the museum.
We stand before the vitrine of the throat
and press our palms to the glass
that separates the scream
from the ear it was meant for—

and still, *still,*
the severed thing keeps speaking,
not in language but in the shape
language leaves when it is taken:
a red word,
weighed and wrapped,
handed down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a poem in the tradition of Black experimental poetry (think M. NourbeSe Philip or Terrance Hayes) that opens with a scientific parasite name in italics and builds through a series of "when" clauses toward a question about who will speak for mutilated flesh.
counterfactuals.output:
*Schistosoma haematobium*

when the fluke enters the water where the children wash,
when the water remembers the river remembers the ship,
when the blood in the urine writes its own red testament
        and no one is fluent,
when the microscope leans down like a colonial eye
        to name what it has already ruined,

when the parasite is given the Latin
        but the host is given nothing,
        not even the dignity of a verb,

when the flesh is counted before it is called,
        when the flesh is charted, cross-sectioned,
        sold to the journal, the grant, the abstract,
when the flesh becomes data becomes distance becomes
        a footnote in a country that will not say its name,

when the mouth is a wound and the wound is a mouth
        and both are open, both are asking,

when the doctor writes *lesion* where the mother would write *my son*,
when history is a species that feeds on the soft interior,
        burrowing, laying its eggs in the walls of us,

when the archive keeps the specimen but loses the person,
when we are preserved in formaldehyde but not in memory—

        who will speak for the mutilated flesh?
        who will decline it like a noun with a soul,
        who will hold the tongue that the water took,
        who will stand at the edge of the ruined river
                and answer in the first person,
                and answer,
                        and answer?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose poem exploring silence, language, and the body as evidence of atrocity. Braid together images of a parasitic tongue louse, a lynched man on a windmill, biblical names, unharvested corn, and a marketplace butcher.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cymothoa

There is a fish that swallows a small crustacean and the crustacean eats the tongue and becomes the tongue and the fish lives on, speaking through what devoured it. This is the first thing. Remember it when I tell you the mouth is not a safe house.

---

They named him something from the book—Absalom, maybe, caught by the hair, or Ishmael, who was heard by God in the wilderness. The names come easy. The names were always the cheapest part. What hung from the windmill's arm turned slowly in a wind that asked nothing, answered nothing, a body making its own slow gospel of revolution: rising, cresting, falling, rising. The blades did not stop. Grain still needed grinding. Somewhere below, the wheel turned water into work.

---

And the corn stood unharvested in the field beside him, gold going to rot, each ear a mouth stuffed with its own gold teeth, silent, silked over, bowing in the same wind that turned the man. Who would harvest under such a shadow? The corn kept its counsel. The corn knew how to be a witness that says nothing, that only stands and browns and falls back into the ground it came from, feeding what comes next with the memory of having seen.

---

I want to tell you about the butcher in the market, how his hands knew every seam in a body, every place the muscle releases the bone. How he wrapped the cuts in paper and the paper drank the red and the women carried it home in baskets and this was called *provision*, this was called *feeding the family*, and no one screamed because the screaming had already happened, elsewhere, in the pen, in the field, on the windmill, in the long night of the name.

---

The louse in the mouth. The tongue that is not a tongue. This is how atrocity learns to speak: it eats the true voice and installs itself in the socket and moves when you move your jaw and you think *I am speaking* but it is the parasite tasting your bread. This is how a country talks about its dead. Fluently. Without a stammer. The stolen tongue does excellent work.

---

Silence, then, is not the absence of the word. Silence is the corn that refuses to be language, that will not translate the man into a lesson, that stands in the field holding its gold and rotting rather than lie. Silence is the body itself, the only document that cannot be revised, the flesh that hangs and says *this happened to a shape exactly like your shape.*

---

The butcher wipes his knife. The blades keep turning. The book is full of names for the beloved and the cast-out and God does not stop them from meaning both at once.

And I open my mouth to tell you and I feel it move—
the small thing that lives where my voice used to be—
and I do not know, I cannot know,
whether these are my words
or only the sounds
the devourer makes
when it wants
to be fed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something raw and difficult about the impossibility of testimony after racial terror—use the tongue-eating louse as an epigraph-like image, employ colons instead of line breaks, and end mid-thought on "as all severed tongues do:"
counterfactuals.output:
The tongue-eating louse enters through the gills, consumes the tongue, then becomes the tongue: this is not metaphor: this is instruction:

They ask me to speak of it: as if speech were a thing left intact: as if the mouth that survived were the same mouth: as if what crawled in after did not already wear my language like a stolen coat: I open my jaw and the parasite answers: fluent, obliging, terrible in its competence:

Consider what testimony demands: a subject who was there: a subject who remained: but the terror was precisely the unmaking of the there, the who, the remained: they burned the courthouse where the record would be kept: they burned the record: they burned the hand that would have written it: and I am asked to be that hand now, reaching up from ash, and I reach, and something reaches for me:

You want the fact of it: the man, the rope, the crowd in Sunday clothes, the postcard sold for a penny: I can give you the postcard: the archive is generous with postcards: what I cannot give you is the interior of the throat that closed: the last word he did not get to make: it is gone: it was eaten: what speaks in its place is smooth, is adapted, has learned to eat what I eat, to say what soothes you, to perform the very grief that proves I have recovered enough to perform it:

This is the trap: to be believed I must be legible: to be legible I must use the tongue that replaced the tongue: the colonizer's grammar, the historian's cool apparatus, the workshop's tidy volta: and every one of these is the louse, is fluent, is me now, indistinguishable:

So understand what I am doing when I open my mouth: I am not remembering: I am being spoken by the thing that ate the memory: and it is very good: it will move you: it will win the prize: it will convince the committee that healing is possible and the nation may proceed:

But there was a boy: there was a boy: I keep beginning with the boy because the beginning is the only part the louse cannot mimic, the raw fork before language, and even now I feel it turning in my throat, hungry, patient, ready to finish this sentence for me as all severed tongues do:
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
